full_judgment: 3. Mr Tawfique Nawaz, the learned Senior Advocate appeared on behalf of the petitioner and submitted that in the report dated 9-9-02 by Technical Evaluation Committee, the respondent No. 8 was disqualified and such technical disqualification precluded respondent No. 8 from having its financial offer opened but in spite of that its financial bid was opened. The two members who had not signed the Technical Evaluation Report dated 9-9-02 were shown to have submitted their reports subsequently and separately. When the work order was issued on 22-9-02 the respondent No.8 did not meet the technical specification of the Covert feature of cigarette stamp and band and even the sample provided at a later stage by the respondent No. 8 was without the covert feature as required. The learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner has further submitted that the work order was issued to respondent No. 8 who did not make a responsive bid. The work order issued on 22-9-2002 contained changed terms with regard to price i.e. conversion, from real value "to token value" and from 'supply' to 'loan'. According to the learned Counsel, the action was malafide, lacked transparency causing exposure to counterfeiting of stamp and band, loss of national revenue and undermining the rule law. Mr Tawfique Nawaz also submitted that respondent Nos. 1-7 acted without lawful authority within the scope of Article 102 of the Constitution and their arbitrary action of treating the minority report of Dr Maksud Helal to prevail over the view of the majority members, in total disregard of the rules and norms relating to decision by the committee is ultra vires, malafide and arbitrary. Mr Tawfique Nawaz drew our attention to the fact that even on 31-10-02 long after the issuance of the work order dated 22-9-02, the respondent Nos. 1-7 continued to fail to meet or cause to meet the Covert security feature of the stamp and band and therefore acted unlawfully and failed to produce before this court the letter dated 31-8-2002 denying approval of sample addressed to respondent No. 8. He has further submitted that respondent No. 7 admitted in his affidavit-in- opposition that the statements made in paragraph 11 of the writ petition are statements of fact and called for no comment and thus, according to the learned Counsel, it is evident that respondent No. 7 has admitted the petitioners' case in fact. Mr Tawfique Nawaz drew our attention to Article 144 of the Constitution which deals with the Executive Authority in relation to property, trade, etc. He has cited a decision as reported in AIR 1996 SC 11 Tata Cellular vs Union of India, in which requirements of tender, principle of judicial review applicable to contractual power exercisablte by government were discussed and was held that terms of the invitation to tender cannot be opened to judicial scrutiny because the invitation to tender is in the realm of contract. He has also referred the judgment delivered in Ekushey Television Ltd and others vs Dr Chowdhury Mahmood Hasan and others as reported in 2002 BLD (AD) 163 = 54 DLR (AD) 130. He referred another decision as reported in 54 DLR (AD) 88 Hyundai Corporation vs Simiking Busamto impress upon us that the present writ may be treated as public interest litigation. Lastly, he has also submitted that though the members of the Board of Directors of the Company took the decision but the Board of Directors comprises of the Governor of Bangladesh Bank and other officers and after referring sections 10(6)/10(8)/16(18) of Bangladesh Bank Order (President's Order 127 of 1972) he has argued that the Chairman and members of the Board of Directors acted for and on behalf of Bangladesh Bank and, as such, they performed the function of a statutory body and thus, according to him, writ is very much maintainable.
